terms.definition: AWS object storage service. Files (objects) are stored in containers called buckets. Used as the origin for static website hosting.
terms.example: Like a hard drive in the cloud — store and retrieve any file using a URL.

terms.definition: S3 feature that enables serving HTML, CSS, JS, and image files directly to browsers via an HTTP endpoint. Does not support server-side code.
terms.example: A portfolio website with HTML pages and CSS — perfect for S3 hosting.

terms.definition: AWS's Content Delivery Network (CDN) service. Caches content at 400+ global edge locations to reduce latency for users worldwide.
terms.example: Like pre-stocking a product in warehouses near your customers instead of shipping from one factory every time.

terms.definition: A system of distributed servers that cache content closer to end users, reducing load time and latency.
terms.example: Netflix uses CDNs so your movie loads from a nearby server, not from Netflix HQ.

terms.definition: Mini data centres distributed globally by CloudFront. They cache content close to end users for fast delivery. Different from AWS Regions and Availability Zones.
terms.example: An edge location in Sydney serves Australian users — no need to fetch from Mumbai every time.

terms.definition: A CloudFront security feature that restricts S3 bucket access so only a specific CloudFront distribution can read it. Keeps the S3 bucket private from the public internet.
terms.example: Like a VIP pass — only the CloudFront bouncer with the right ID gets into the S3 club.

terms.definition: A CloudFront deployment unit. Each distribution gets a unique domain name (dxxxxx.cloudfront.net), links to one or more origins, and defines caching behaviour.
terms.example: You create one CloudFront distribution per website or application you want to accelerate.

terms.definition: How long CloudFront caches an object at an edge location before checking the origin for a fresh copy. Default is 86,400 seconds (24 hours).
terms.example: If TTL is 24 hours, CloudFront will serve a cached file for up to 24 hours before fetching an updated version from S3.

terms.definition: When a user requests a file and CloudFront already has it cached at the nearest edge location. The file is served instantly without contacting the origin.
terms.example: The first visitor fetches from S3 (cache miss), the second visitor gets it from the edge (cache hit) — much faster.

terms.definition: When a user requests a file that is NOT cached at the edge location. CloudFront fetches it from the origin (S3), caches it, then serves it.
terms.example: The very first request for a new file is always a cache miss — subsequent requests are cache hits.

terms.definition: AWS's authoritative DNS (Domain Name System) service. Translates domain names into IP addresses and supports multiple routing policies for traffic management.
terms.example: Like a phone book — you look up 'www.amazon.com' and it tells you the IP address to connect to.

terms.definition: The internet's naming system. Translates human-readable domain names (www.example.com) into machine-readable IP addresses.
terms.example: Without DNS, you would have to type 192.0.2.44 instead of www.example.com.

terms.definition: A Route 53 container for DNS records for a specific domain. Route 53 assigns 4 name servers to each hosted zone.
terms.example: Create a hosted zone for 'mycompany.com' and add records to control where traffic goes.

terms.definition: The servers that answer DNS queries for your domain. Route 53 assigns 4 name servers per hosted zone. You configure these at your domain registrar.
terms.example: ns-123.awsdns-45.com — enter these at GoDaddy/Namecheap to make Route 53 authoritative for your domain.

terms.definition: An AWS-specific DNS record type in Route 53. Works like a CNAME but can be used at the zone apex (example.com) and is free for queries pointing to AWS resources.
terms.example: Point example.com (not just www.example.com) directly to a CloudFront distribution using an ALIAS record.

terms.definition: A DNS record that maps one domain name to another. Cannot be used at the zone apex. Standard across all DNS providers.
terms.example: Map blog.example.com to example.wordpress.com using a CNAME.

terms.definition: The official AWS SDK for Python. Provides both high-level (resource) and low-level (client) interfaces to all AWS services.
terms.example: Write Python code to automatically launch EC2 instances, upload files to S3, or send messages via SQS.

terms.definition: Software Development Kit — a set of programming libraries that lets developers interact with AWS services from application code without using the console or CLI.
terms.example: A mobile app uses the AWS SDK to upload user photos directly to S3 from the app code.

terms.definition: A pre-configured OS image used to launch EC2 instances. AMI IDs are region-specific — the same OS has a different AMI ID in each AWS region.
terms.example: The Ubuntu Server 22.04 AMI ID in Mumbai (ap-south-1) is different from the same Ubuntu AMI in Singapore (ap-southeast-1).

terms.definition: A process to immediately remove specific files from all CloudFront edge caches before their TTL expires, forcing CloudFront to fetch fresh versions from the origin.
terms.example: You update your website's CSS file. Create an invalidation for /style.css to clear the cached old version instantly.

terms.definition: Web files that are the same for every user — HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, PDFs. No server-side processing needed.
terms.example: A company homepage with product photos and a contact form is static content.

terms.definition: A JSON-based access policy attached to an S3 bucket that defines who can perform which actions on the bucket and its objects.
terms.example: A bucket policy with Principal:* and Action:s3:GetObject opens a bucket for public read access.
